title: How can an owl see without moving its eyes?

segments.text: There's a bird that, unbelievably, can't move its eyes at all, yet it sees everything around it. Which animal can do that? An owl.
Its eyes are tubes, locked in place by rings of bone, so it has to turn its whole head to look around.
It can twist that head up to {270|two hundred seventy} degrees. Try that and the arteries in your neck could tear.
But owls have {14|fourteen} neck bones, twice as many as you, plus blood vessels with backup pools that keep the brain supplied mid-twist.
Up close, though, they're nearly blind. So an owl feels its food with fine feathers around the beak.
Its real superpower is hearing. One ear sits higher than the other, and the flat face funnels sound like a satellite dish. A great gray owl can hear a mouse under deep snow, then dive in to catch it.
And you'd never hear it coming. Comb-like feather edges break up the air, making flight nearly silent. Engineers copy them for quieter wind turbines.
So an owl can't move its eyes. It just moves everything else. Follow for a weird everyday truth daily.
